name: Syndicalism
info: Syndicalism is a revolutionary socialist current that organised workers by industry into unions meant to win demands by direct action and strikes and to bring about workers' control of production; it rose to prominence in France and spread across several continents.

facts.thinkers: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, whose mutualism was its direct root; Mikhail Bakunin, who advocated the general strike; Émile Pouget, anarchist and CGT leader who backed sabotage and direct action; Victor Griffuelhes of the CGT; Bill Haywood and Vincent St. John of the IWW; James Larkin of the Irish ITGWU; Tom Mann of Britain; Rudolf Rocker, who wrote the FAUD's programme; Georges Sorel, whose Reflections on Violence brought syndicalist ideas to a wider audience
facts.texts: The Charter of Amiens (adopted by the CGT in 1906); Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence (English edition 1912); Ford and Foster, Syndicalism (1913); the Industrial Workers of the World, The IWW: What it is and what it is not (1928); Rudolf Rocker, Anarcho-syndicalism: Theory and Practice (1938)
facts.ideas: irreconcilable class struggle between workers and the bourgeoisie; unions as both organs of struggle within capitalism and the embryo of a new society; direct action, sabotage and above all the general strike; independence of unions from political parties; federalism over centralism; replacement of the state by workers' organisations; production managed by the workers
facts.today: The International Workers' Association (IWA–AIT) exists with very little influence; the Spanish CNT had around 50,000 members in 2018 and the CGT, which split from it, around 100,000; the German FAU, the British Solidarity Federation and Sweden's SAC Syndikalisterna carry on the tradition; the International Confederation of Labour was formed in 2018

t: Syndicalists held that unions, not political parties, should wage the class struggle by direct action and the general strike, and that union federations would manage production and replace the state after a revolution.

Syndicalist organisations such as the CGT in France, the CNT in Spain, the USI in Italy, the FAUD in Germany and the FORA in Argentina reached their height between about 1910 and the early 1920s, and in Spain from 1936 put much of the economy under workers' control until the Nationalist victory.

Scholars disagree on the word itself: some apply it to every revolutionary, direct-action union movement, including the IWW, while others, such as Larry Peterson, use five criteria that exclude the IWW and the Canadian One Big Union.
dyk: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, a root of syndicalist thought, coined the word capitalist, and Émile Pouget said that the idea of the general strike came to France from the United States, fertilised by the blood of the anarchists hanged in Chicago.
ev: The French General Confederation of Labour (CGT) is formed; it advocates the general strike from the start
The Industrial Workers of the World is founded in the United States
The CGT adopts the Charter of Amiens, reaffirming its independence from party politics
The Italian syndicalist confederation USI is formed by veterans of the farm and factory strikes
The First International Syndicalist Congress meets in London but does not found an international
The Free Workers' Union of Germany (FAUD) is formed in December
The International Workers' Association is formed as an international syndicalist federation
The Spanish Revolution puts much of Spain's economy under workers' control, with the CNT as the main union organisation of the Republican side

sections.origins:
Syndicalism is a revolutionary socialist current within the labour movement. The word comes from the French syndicat, a trade union, and the concept of syndicalisme révolutionnaire emerged in French socialist journals in 1903, when the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) came to use it for its own brand of unionism. Its direct roots lay in Pierre-Joseph Proudhon's mutualism, popular in the anti-authoritarian wing of the International Workingmen's Association formed in 1864. Its leader Mikhail Bakunin came to believe that worker organisations might need to use force; he and his followers advocated the general strike, rejected electoral politics and anticipated workers' organisations replacing rule by the state. Lucien van der Walt holds that the Spanish Regional Federation of that International, formed in 1870, was already syndicalist.

The Haymarket Affair in Chicago in 1886 led anarchists and labour organisers in the United States and Europe to rethink the revolutionary meaning of the general strike. In the 1890s French anarchists, concluding that individual action such as assassination had failed, turned to the labour movement and gained influence in the bourses du travail, which formed a national federation in 1893. The CGT was formed in 1895 and advocated the general strike from the start; the bourses merged into it in 1902, and in 1906 it adopted the Charter of Amiens.
sections.ideas:
Syndicalists held that society was divided into two classes, the working class and the bourgeoisie, whose interests were irreconcilable. Tom Mann declared that the object of the unions was to wage the Class War, aimed not only at higher wages or shorter hours but at the revolutionary overthrow of capitalism. They agreed with Marx that the state was the executive committee of the ruling class, and held that an economic order could not be overthrown by changes to the political order. Unions therefore declared their political neutrality, on the reasoning that parties united members of different classes while unions united the whole working class.

Unions played a dual role: they fought for immediate improvements within capitalism and were to carry out the revolution. Syndicalists favoured direct action, among them working to rule, passive resistance, sabotage and strikes, and saw the general strike as the final step towards revolution. They remained vague about the society to follow, saying it could not be foreseen in detail, but generally agreed that production would be managed by workers and the state apparatus replaced by the rule of workers' organisations, with the unions as the embryo of the new society. Many rejected collective bargaining agreements and large strike funds for fear of bureaucracy.

Policies on gender were mixed. The CNT did not admit women until 1918, and the CGT dismissed feminism as a bourgeois movement, though attitudes shifted in some cases.
sections.spread:
French syndicalism and American industrial unionism influenced its rise elsewhere. Activists who had spent time in France founded syndicalist organisations in Hungary, Spain and Italy, Émile Pouget's pamphlets were translated into several languages, and migrants and sailors carried the ideas to other countries. The Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) was formed in 1905 in the United States; its members insisted theirs was a distinctly American unionism, though most IWW historians, such as Melvyn Dubofsky, regard it as the American form of syndicalism. The Argentine Regional Workers' Federation (FORA) was formed by Italian and Spanish immigrants in 1901.

Some syndicalists worked within existing unions; others built federations of their own, a strategy known as dual unionism, as with the IWW, the Irish Transport and General Workers' Union, the Italian USI and the Spanish CNT. By 1914 there were syndicalist national confederations in Peru, Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, the Netherlands, Germany, Sweden, Spain, Italy and France.

The First International Syndicalist Congress met in London in 1913 with 38 delegates from 65 organisations but founded no international. When the First World War began, most syndicalists opposed it, but the majority of the CGT and a minority of the USI, led by Alceste De Ambris, supported their countries. The International Workers' Association followed in 1922.
sections.power:
Syndicalist movements seldom held power and were mostly under pressure from states and rival socialists. In Mexico the syndicalist Casa del Obrero Mundial allied with the government established after the Constitutionalist Army occupied the capital in 1914, helping to defeat rural forces such as the Zapatistas, but the army quelled its general strike of July and August 1916 and the Casa was suppressed. In Russia syndicalists welcomed the soviets and factory committees of 1917, and workers' control was introduced, but it led to economic chaos and the Bolsheviks put the economy under state control and subordinated the committees to trade unions that became organs of the state. Syndicalists, who denounced the regime as state capitalist, were harassed and arrested, and the arrests that followed the Kronstadt rebellion of 1921 ended the movement.

The widest application came in Spain. The Spanish Revolution of 1936 brought anarcho-syndicalist and more broadly socialist organisational principles to Catalonia, Aragon, Andalusia and parts of the Levante for two to three years, with the CNT the main union organisation of the Republican side, and much of the economy was put under workers' control before the Nationalists won the civil war and suppressed them.

Elsewhere repression was severe. In Brazil some 200 workers were killed in São Paulo alone in 1917 to 1919, and in Argentina between 100 and 700 people died in the Tragic Week of 1919.
sections.critiques:
Within the labour movement the main attacks came from socialists and communists. Vladimir Lenin posited that revolutionary syndicalism was a direct and inevitable result of opportunism, reformism and parliamentary cretinism. According to many Marxists, syndicalism was a reaction to reformism and could not survive without it. Darlington holds that communism exposed syndicalism's inherent weaknesses: building organisations meant to be both revolutionary cadres and mass unions, stressing economic struggle over political action, and a commitment to localism that limited effective central leadership. The anarchist Iain McKay argues that syndicalism is a new name for the ideas of Bakunin and the anarchist wing of the First International, and wholly inconsistent with Marx and Engels.

Historians dispute how far its doctrines were shared by members. Peter Stearns concludes that most French workers did not identify with its long-range goals, while Frederick Ridley holds that it was a genuine product of the French labour movement. Stearns also judged French syndicalism a dismal failure, arguing that its radicalism shocked workers and the government and weakened the movement as a whole. Robert Hoxie, Selig Perlman and Patrick Renshaw attribute the IWW's decline to workers' pragmatism, a view Darlington disputes.

Georges Sorel was often thought its premier theorist, but he was not part of the movement and his influence was insignificant except in Italy and Poland.
sections.legacy:
From the early 1920s syndicalist movements waned in most countries. Authoritarian governments suppressed them in Russia, Italy, Portugal, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands, and the IWW and the Mexican Casa were weakened by repression. Van der Linden and Thorpe attribute the decline of those not suppressed mainly to the integration of the working class into capitalist relations, helped by the welfare state and the widening of the franchise. Eric Hobsbawm saw the rise of communism as the biggest reason. By the end of the 1930s meaningful legal syndicalist organisations existed only in Bolivia, Chile, Sweden and Uruguay. The Nationalist victory in Spain ended it as a mass movement.

The IWA still exists, with very little influence; Wayne Thorpe called it a flicker of history, the custodian of doctrine. The CNT peaked at over 300,000 members in 1978, then split, and the breakaway CGT had around 100,000 members in 2018. The CNT and the German FAU left the IWA in 2018 to form the International Confederation of Labour. The late 1960s revived interest among activists in Germany, the United States and Britain, and in the 1980s the Polish union Solidarity, though not strictly syndicalist, revived many of its ideas and practices.

Darlington notes that the IWW song Solidarity Forever entered the American labour canon, and that the sit-down strike, made famous at Flint, was pioneered by Wobblies in 1906.

summary: Syndicalism is a revolutionary current of the labour movement, taking shape in France in the 1890s and 1900s, that looked to industrial unions, direct action and the general strike to overthrow capitalism and put production under workers' control. It peaked before and after the First World War and in Spain in 1936, then declined under repression and the rise of communism and social democracy.
references: Ralph Darlington, Syndicalism and the Transition to Communism: An International Comparative Analysis (Ashgate Publishing, 2008)
Frederick Ridley, Revolutionary Syndicalism in France: The Direct Action of its Time (Cambridge University Press, 1970)
Wayne Thorpe, 'The Workers Themselves': Revolutionary Syndicalism and International Labour, 1913–1923 (Kluwer, 1989)
Lucien van der Walt, Black Flame: The Revolutionary Class Politics of Anarchism and Syndicalism (AK Press, 2009)
notes: Start 1895, circa true: the article dates the CGT's formation to 1895 (advocating the general strike from the start), the concept to 1903 and the IWW to 1905, and says some syndicalist practices predate the term; Lucien van der Walt calls the Spanish Regional Federation of 1870 syndicalist, which I give as his view and do not use as the start.
Scope of the term is disputed (Darlington, van der Linden and Thorpe broad; Peterson and Olssen narrow); the article's own opening says unions first emerged in Spain and North America in the 1870s.
Sorel's Reflections on Violence is given in the article's Further reading as 1912 (New York edition).
The 1913 congress: the article gives dates 27 September to 2 October with year 1913 only in the surrounding sentences.
